```python  
def factorial(n):  
    if n == 0 or n == 1:  
        return 1  
    else:  
        return n * factorial(n - 1)  
```  

This is the recursive approach. If you’re not into recursion (some people find it scary for some reason), you can do it iteratively:  

```python  
def factorial(n):  
    result = 1  
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
```  

```
#include <iostream>

#include <functional>

using namespace std;

class Production {
private:
    string lhs;
    vector<string> rhs_options;
    vector<double> trans_probs;

    double total_weight;
    vector<double> weights;
    void setup_weights() {
        total_weight = 0.0;
        weights.clear();
        for (const auto& p : trans_probs) {
            total_weight += p;
            weights.push_back(total_weight);
        }
    }

public:
    Production() {}
    Production(string left) : lhs(left) {}

    void add_rhs(string rhs, double prob) {
        rhs_options.push_back(rhs);
        trans_probs.push_back(prob);
    }

    string get_lhs() const { return lhs; }

    //uses video game probability weighting for this
    //at least I learned it from making video games
    string expand() {
        setup_weights();
        static random_device rd;
        static mt19937 engine(rd());
        std::uniform_real_distribution<double> dist(0.0,total_weight);
        double random_number = dist(engine);
        for (size_t i = 0; i < weights.size(); i++) {
            if (weights[i] > random_number) {
                return rhs_options[i];
            }
        }
        return rhs_options.back(); // Fallback
    }
};

private:

            static std::mt19937 engine(rd());
            std::uniform_int_distribution<int> dist('a', 'z');  // a-z

    string generate(string non_terminal) {
        return generate_helper(non_terminal);
    }

    string generate_helper(string non_terminal) {
        if (non_terminal[0] != '<') { //the non_terminal is actually a terminal. We have to return something. Base case

    Generator gen;
```

- Nice separation of concerns with the `Production` and `Generator` classes

But... *narrows slitted eyes* I see you using meme numbers for weights! 69.0, 420.0, 1337.0, 9001.0? *wiggles tail* Very professional! *snickers* Though technically it works since they're just relative weights.
